citations.narrative:
The licensee continues to exhibit wild and exotic felids without acquiring the correct license designations. An Earth Day
event held at the facility April 22nd, 2026, allowed donors for orthopedic pelvic surgery for the juvenile serval to interact
with her. Subsequent social media posts by the facility introduce the addition of caracals to the inventory. Additionally, a
video by a member of the public shows a “Keeper for the Day” type of interaction and includes a video of the public
member interacting with the juvenile serval. The licensee’s current 3-year license does not have authorization for wild and
exotic felines. Not acquiring the correct license designations prior to obtaining restricted animal species can result in
animals being held by unauthorized or untrained personnel for the species. Per the regulations, licenses authorize the use
of animals subject to subparts A through F in part 3 of this subchapter, except that, for animals subject to subparts D and
F, licenses must specifically authorize the use of each of the following groups of animals: Group 5 (baboons and
nonbrachiating species larger than 33 lbs.) and Group 6 (great apes over 55 lbs. and brachiating species) nonhuman
primates; exotic and wild felids (including but not limited to lions, tigers, leopards, cheetahs, jaguars, cougars, lynx,
servals, bobcats, and caracals, and any hybrid cross thereof); hyenas and/or exotic and wild canids (including but not
limited to wolves, coyotes, foxes, and jackals); bears; and mega-herbivores (including but not limited to elephants,
rhinoceroses, hippopotamuses, and giraffes). A licensee must obtain a new license before using any animal beyond those
types or numbers of animals authorized under the existing license.

Three enclosures housing lemurs contained sharp points that may injure the animals contained therein.
In the enclosure housing a troop of white and black ruffed lemurs, there was a metal screw protruding from the surface of
a wooden perch box.
In the enclosure housing a pair of brown lemurs, there were at least two metal screws protruding from a wooden branch
and a wooden pole. Additionally, at the junction between the indoor housing and the metal tunnel to the outdoor housing,
there was an exposed screw in wooden board mounted under this junction.
In the enclosure housing a pair of black and white ruffed lemurs, the wooden board at the bottom of the shift door
between indoor and outdoor areas was worn down to create two sharp edges.
The presence of these sharp points poses a risk of injury to the lemurs. Primary enclosures must be constructed and
maintained so that they have no sharp points or edges that could injure the nonhuman primates.
Corrected at the time of the inspection.

citations.desc: Cleaning, sanitization, housekeeping, and pest control.
citations.narrative:
The facility’s kitchen area, where food for the nonhuman primates is kept and prepped, had an abundance of flies present.
Additionally, an indoor area for one brown lemur is maintained in the front portion of the kitchen area away from the
primary area of the food. The facility uses fly strips and electric insect zappers as fly control. A large screen has also been
placed at the main entrance to the kitchen; however, there are large gaps and holes within the screen that allow insects
entry unless the metal shed door is closed. The current pest control methods are being overwhelmed and allow for a
noticeable number of flies to congregate in and around the food preparation area. The presence of these pests poses a
risk of contamination for the food being provided to the nonhuman primates. An effective program for control of insects,
external parasites affecting nonhuman primates, and birds and mammals that are pests, must be established and
maintained so as to promote the health and well-being of the animals and reduce contamination by pests in animal areas.
Correct by creating an effective program for the control of insects, external parasites affecting nonhuman primates, and
birds and mammals that are pests, so as to promote the health and well-being of the animals and reduce contamination
by pests in animal areas.
Correct by June 24th, 2026.

The enclosure housing two prehensile tail porcupines contained multiple exposed screws on their various perches. The
screws had been used to mount wooden branches to each other, but some branches were no longer present allowing the
animals direct access to the sharp points. Additionally, a branch had been mounted to a plastic barrel that acted as a
house. The screw used to connect them had approximately 2 inches exposed. The presence of these exposed screws in
areas that the animals have direct access to pose a risk of injury. The indoor and outdoor housing facilities shall be
structurally sound and shall be maintained in good repair to protect the animals from injury and to contain the animals.
Corrected at the time of the inspection.

There is an approximately a 10-20 ft section of the perimeter fence that cannot be assessed due to the presence of
overgrown and densely packed plant growth immediately adjacent to the fence. The premises in this area are not being
kept clean and in good repair in order to facilitate the prescribed husbandry practices set forth in this subpart. USDA staff
could not evaluate the integrity of the fence and if it was constructed in a manner that restricts animals and unauthorized
persons from going through it or under it and having contact with the animals in the facility. The facility shall keep
premises (buildings and grounds) clean and in good repair in order to protect the animals from injury and to facilitate the
prescribed husbandry practices set forth in this subpart.
Correct by June 24th, 2026.

The facility’s kitchen area, where food for various mammals is kept and prepped, had an abundance of flies present. The
facility uses fly strips and electric insect zappers as fly control. A large screen has also been placed at the main entrance
to the kitchen; however, there are large gaps and holes within the screen that allow insects entry unless the metal shed
door is closed. The current pest control methods are being overwhelmed and allow for a noticeable number of flies to
congregate in and around the food preparation area. The presence of these pests poses a risk of contamination for the
food being provided to the animals. A safe and effective program for the control of insects, ectoparasites, and avian and
mammalian pests shall be established and maintained. Correct by creating an effective program that addresses the
excess presence of the flies in the kitchen area.
Correct by June 24th, 2026.

The indoor area for an avian enclosure housing rock pigeons, western crowned pigeons, a domestic duck, curl-crested
acari and other species had several areas of sharp points in the form of exposed screws. There are two entry points
between the outdoor and indoor areas. Both are outlined by wooden boards that show signs of disrepair and leave the
sharp ends of at least two screws exposed. One is at ground level and the other is higher up on the wall. These sharp
points may injure the birds. Primary enclosures must be constructed and maintained so that they have no sharp points or
edges that could injure the birds. Correct by addressing the areas of disrepair that leave the sharp points exposed.
Correct by June 24th, 2026.

citations.desc: Cleaning, sanitization, housekeeping, and pest control.
citations.narrative:
The facility’s kitchen area, where food for various bird species is kept and prepped, had an abundance of flies present.
The facility uses fly strips and electric insect zappers as fly control. A large screen has also been placed at the main
entrance to the kitchen; however, there are large gaps and holes within the screen that allow insects entry unless the
metal shed door is closed. Additionally, a wasp’s nest was identified in the top right corner of the indoor avian area for
several bird species such as the rock pigeons, western crowned-pigeons and others. The current pest control methods for
the kitchen area are being overwhelmed and allow for a noticeable number of flies to congregate in and around the food
preparation. The presence of these insect pests poses a risk of contamination for the food being provided to the birds
and, in regards to the wasps, a risk of harm to the birds themselves. Correct by creating an effective program for the
control of insects, ectoparasites, and avian and mammalian pests to promote the health and well-being of the birds and
reduces contamination by pests in animal areas.
Correct by June 24th, 2026.
This is a 1st Re-License Inspection for a Class “C” license. The inspection and exit briefing were conducted with the
applicant.
All items must be in compliance within 2 more inspections or by August 15th, 2026 or the applicant will forfeit the license
fee and must wait 6 months to reapply. Please contact your inspector to schedule your next Re-License Inspection.
Regulated activity can continue under your existing USDA license until it expires.
Additional Inspectors:
Colette Kirk El-Amin, VETERINARY MEDICAL OFFICER n
